items.name: Rule of thirds
items.description: Divide the frame into a three-by-three grid and place the subject or key features, such as the eyes or the horizon, on the lines or where they cross.
items.when_to_use: Default framing for portraits, landscapes and most coverage when you want a natural, balanced image without centring.
items.effect: Feels natural and easy on the eye; leaves room for the subject to look or move into and keeps attention on the subject.

items.name: Leading lines
items.description: Use real or implied lines in the scene, such as roads, corridors, fences or gazes, to pull the eye towards the subject or a point of interest.
items.when_to_use: When you need to steer attention, add depth to a flat frame, or point towards a destination, threat or character.
items.effect: Creates direction, momentum and depth; can suggest journey, inevitability or being drawn towards something.

items.name: Symmetry and central framing
items.description: Place the subject on the centre axis with both halves of the frame mirroring each other, or close to it.
items.when_to_use: For formal, stylised or ritual moments, institutions, confrontations and strong stand-alone portraits.
items.effect: Reads as order, control, stillness or unease; deliberate symmetry feels designed and can be authoritative, comic or eerie.

items.name: Frame within a frame
items.description: Shoot the subject through a doorway, window, arch or other foreground shape so a second frame sits inside the picture frame.
items.when_to_use: To focus the eye, show confinement or observation, or add layers to a simple location.
items.effect: Isolation, entrapment, voyeurism or privileged view; draws attention and adds depth.

items.name: Negative space
items.description: Leave a large, mostly empty area around a small subject so the emptiness becomes part of the composition.
items.when_to_use: To show loneliness, scale, tension before an arrival, or to make a conversation feel awkward by how people sit in the frame.
items.effect: Isolation, vulnerability, calm or unease; the empty area asks the viewer to wonder what is missing or what will enter.

items.name: Depth and foreground layering
items.description: Arrange elements in foreground, middle ground and background so the 2D image reads as a deep space.
items.when_to_use: Establishing shots, busy locations, and any time a flat frame needs dimension; foreground objects can also half-hide the subject.
items.effect: Immersion and realism; layers can add voyeurism (looking past something) or show relationships between planes of action.

items.name: Looking room and short siding
items.description: Leave more empty space in the direction a character looks or moves (looking room); the opposite, putting them close to the edge they face, is short siding.
items.when_to_use: Looking room for natural dialogue and anticipation; short siding for claustrophobia, threat or a character who feels cornered.
items.effect: Looking room gives openness and anticipation; short siding gives tension, entrapment or something looming off-screen.

items.name: Headroom
items.description: The amount of space between the top of a subject's head and the top of the frame; normally small but not zero, and varied by shot size.
items.when_to_use: Set it for every figure shot; trim it for intimacy and give extra when you want the character to seem small or exposed.
items.effect: Tight headroom feels intense, intimate or oppressive; generous headroom feels relaxed, exposed or dwarfed by surroundings.

items.name: Balance and visual weight
items.description: Distribute visual weight (size, brightness, colour, faces) so the frame feels stable, or deliberately unbalance it.
items.when_to_use: Balanced frames for stability; lopsided frames to hint at conflict, a missing element or a power gap between characters.
items.effect: Balance reads as harmony and rest; imbalance creates tension and a sense that something must change.

items.name: Triangle composition
items.description: Arrange three subjects or points of interest so they form a triangle, a stable shape that also suggests relationships and hierarchy.
items.when_to_use: Group scenes and three-handers; a point at the top can show dominance, a wide base stability.
items.effect: Stability and clear hierarchy; can express alliances, rivalry or a love triangle in the staging itself.

items.name: Golden ratio and spiral
items.description: Divide the frame in the proportion of roughly 1 to 1.618, or follow the spiral derived from it, to place the main interest off-centre in a more organic way than thirds.
items.when_to_use: As a refinement of thirds when planning a still, a hero shot or a carefully designed frame with a clear focal point.
items.effect: A flowing, harmonious pull of the eye towards the focal point, felt as natural rather than rigid.

items.name: Ultra-wide lens
items.description: A very short focal length (roughly 18 mm and under on a full-frame sensor) that takes in a huge field of view and exaggerates perspective.
items.when_to_use: Cramped interiors, sweeping landscapes, action seen from close, or stylised distortion of a face or space.
items.effect: Disorientation, spectacle or intimacy with distortion; objects near the lens loom and distances stretch.

items.name: Wide-angle lens
items.description: A short focal length (roughly 24-35 mm full-frame) with a wide view and strong sense of depth, with less distortion than an ultra-wide.
items.when_to_use: Establishing shots, walk-and-talk, group scenes, and showing a character within their environment.
items.effect: Openness, context and immersion; moving close to the subject adds energy and presence.

items.name: Normal lens (around 50 mm)
items.description: A focal length close to the natural look of human vision, with little perspective distortion.
items.when_to_use: Neutral coverage, dialogue and naturalistic scenes where the lens should not call attention to itself.
items.effect: Honest, grounded, observational; feels like the viewer is simply standing in the scene.

items.name: Telephoto lens
items.description: A long focal length (roughly 70 mm and up) that narrows the view, magnifies distant subjects and compresses the apparent distance between planes.
items.when_to_use: Surveillance feel, tight close-ups from a distance, isolating a subject against a blurred background, or stacking crowds and traffic.
items.effect: Voyeurism, pressure and isolation; compression can make a character feel trapped in a crowd or the background crowd in on them.

items.name: Macro lens
items.description: A lens that focuses very close, reproducing tiny subjects at about life size or larger.
items.when_to_use: Insert shots of small objects, eyes, textures, insects and fine detail the viewer should notice.
items.effect: Heightened attention and intimacy; turns small things into significant ones and can feel tense or wondrous.

items.name: Shallow depth of field
items.description: Only a thin slice of the scene is sharp, usually via a wide aperture, long lens or close subject, so the background and foreground blur.
items.when_to_use: To single out one character, separate them from a busy background, or give a soft, dreamy or intimate look.
items.effect: Focus and intimacy, subjective attention; the blurred world can feel distant or ethereal.

items.name: Deep focus (deep depth of field)
items.description: Foreground, middle ground and background are all sharp, typically from a small aperture, wide lens and plenty of light.
items.when_to_use: Staging in depth, group dynamics, or when the setting matters as much as the actor and the viewer should choose where to look.
items.effect: Realism and a sense of an observable world; lets multiple story layers play inside one shot.

items.name: Rack focus
items.description: Shift the focus during a shot from one subject or distance to another so the sharp plane changes in view.
items.when_to_use: To redirect attention, reveal something in the background, or connect two characters or objects within one take.
items.effect: Directs the audience's attention and shows a change of awareness or a reveal, as if the camera shifts its gaze.

items.name: Split diopter
items.description: A half-lens filter in front of the camera lets near and far subjects be sharp together, with a soft line where the halves meet.
items.when_to_use: When two actions at very different distances matter at once and you want one continuous shot rather than cutting.
items.effect: Unease and tension between planes; a distinctive, slightly uncanny look in which foreground and background compete.

items.name: Anamorphic lens
items.description: A lens that squeezes a wide image onto the sensor, then is de-squeezed in post, giving a widescreen frame, oval bokeh and horizontal flares.
items.when_to_use: For a cinematic widescreen look, epic landscapes, or when you want flares and characteristic out-of-focus shapes.
items.effect: Grand, filmic scale and a dreamy texture; associated with big-screen cinema.

items.name: Tilt-shift lens
items.description: A lens whose optics can tilt or shift to change the plane of focus and correct perspective, so a thin strip is sharp at an angle.
items.when_to_use: Miniature-effect shots of cities, dreamlike sequences, and selective focus across an angled plane.
items.effect: Toy-like or surreal feeling, or a sense of detachment from the scene; rare and therefore very noticeable.

items.name: Three-point lighting
items.description: A standard set-up with a key light as the main source, a fill to soften shadows and a backlight to separate the subject from the background.
items.when_to_use: Interviews, dialogue, and as a baseline to adjust: more fill for a gentle look, less for drama.
items.effect: Clean, readable and flattering; the subject looks dimensional and separate from the background.

items.name: High-key lighting
items.description: Bright, low-contrast lighting with plenty of fill so shadows are light and the overall picture is airy.
items.when_to_use: Comedies, commercials, musicals, cheerful or clinical scenes.
items.effect: Optimism, openness, cleanliness; can feel cheerful or, pushed too far, sterile or falsely perfect.

items.name: Low-key lighting
items.description: Mostly dark frame with strong contrast, little fill and defined pools of light.
items.when_to_use: Thrillers, noir, horror, and any scene of secrecy or danger.
items.effect: Mystery, tension, moral ambiguity and menace; hides information and makes the viewer lean in.

items.name: Chiaroscuro
items.description: Strong contrast of light and deep shadow to model form, borrowed from painting, with parts of the subject falling into darkness.
items.when_to_use: Dramatic portraits, period pieces, interrogation or confession scenes, anything with an inner conflict.
items.effect: Drama, depth and moral conflict; light and dark mirror the character's duality.

items.name: Rembrandt lighting
items.description: A key light placed about 45 degrees to the side and above the face so a small triangle of light shows on the shadowed cheek.
items.when_to_use: Portraits and close-ups when you want a classic, moody and sculpted face.
items.effect: Serious, painterly and dignified; gives depth and mystery to a face.

items.name: Silhouette
items.description: Light the background and keep the subject unlit or backlit so the subject reads as a flat dark shape.
items.when_to_use: Mysterious introductions, striking shapes against sunsets or windows, and hiding identity or emotion.
items.effect: Anonymity, mystery, menace or iconic stillness; the shape speaks while detail is withheld.

items.name: Backlight and rim light
items.description: A light behind the subject, aimed toward the camera, which traces a bright edge on hair and shoulders and separates them from the background.
items.when_to_use: To lift subjects from dark backgrounds, add glow to hair or smoke, or give a character a heroic or ethereal outline.
items.effect: Separation and glow; can read as angelic, heroic, dreamy or eerie.

items.name: Practical lighting
items.description: Use lights that appear in the shot, such as lamps, candles, neon signs and screens, as the actual sources or to carry the look.
items.when_to_use: Realistic interiors and night scenes, or when you want the visible fixtures to define the mood.
items.effect: Authenticity and intimacy; the world seems to be lit by itself, with pools of warm or coloured light.

items.name: Motivated lighting
items.description: Lighting that imitates a believable in-world source, such as a window or lamp, even when the real lights are elsewhere.
items.when_to_use: Whenever the audience should accept the light as natural while you shape it for the shot.
items.effect: Naturalism; the light feels like it belongs to the place and time, not the film crew.

items.name: Hard light vs soft light
items.description: Hard light comes from a small or distant source and makes crisp shadows; soft light is diffused through a large source and wraps gently with soft shadow edges.
items.when_to_use: Hard for drama, texture and harsh conditions; soft for flattering faces, tenderness and gentle mood.
items.effect: Hard feels stark, tense or gritty; soft feels gentle, romantic or flattering.

items.name: Golden hour
items.description: Shoot shortly after sunrise or before sunset when the sun is low and its light is warm, directional and softer.
items.when_to_use: Romantic, nostalgic or hopeful exteriors; a limited time window so plan the schedule around it.
items.effect: Warmth, nostalgia, romance, reflection or an ending; long shadows and a glowing tone.

items.name: Colour contrast (teal and orange)
items.description: Push warm skin tones towards orange and cool the surroundings to teal, using complementary colours so each stands out.
items.when_to_use: For blockbuster-style grading or any scene where a character must pop against a cool environment.
items.effect: Visual punch and separation; warm vs cool can signal human warmth against a cold world.
